title: Brahma Steals the Calves and Boys
story:
Brahma, the lotus-born, had seen it all. From beyond the world he had watched a small cowherd child walk into the open mouth of a python-demon, and he had watched the same child lead his friends out again, alive. He had seen the great light leave the dead demon and enter the boy. The wonder of it would not leave him.

He was the maker of the worlds, the firstborn. He had shaped the stars and set the seasons turning, and nothing in his creation was supposed to surprise him. And yet here was a thing in Vrindavan that his own handiwork could not explain — a village child who had stepped into death and come out holding his friends by the hand. Could it be what it seemed to be? The verses say he wanted to see the beauty of that greatness again, and more besides, and that he wanted to be certain.

So he waited, and the chance came quickly. One day the boys were at their play on a sandbank by the river. It was an ordinary day of the kind Vrindavan knew well — the calves grazing near at hand, the boys spreading out their meal and eating together, the sun warm on the water. In a careless moment the calves strayed, and Krishna went after them alone, to bring them back. The sandbank lay quiet behind him, and the boys, whose sudden fear Krishna had just quieted with a word, were at ease. What was there to fear, with Krishna only a little way off?

And into that quiet Brahma moved. It was not a violent thing. One moment the cowherd boys were there, and the next they were gone, and the calves with them — gathered up and hidden away by a power no one in Vrindavan could see or name. No footfall, no sound; the river went on running as if nothing had been there at all. The creator carried them off as easily as a man gathers a handful of seeds, and set them down in a place beyond the reach of any searching eye. Then he waited to see what the child would do.

When Krishna came back to the sandbank, the river was the only sound. No boys. No calves. The food they had been eating lay where it had been set down, and no one was left to eat it. He knew at once what had happened, and who had done it, for nothing is hidden from him. And yet, the old verses say, he searched. He went into the deep forest and looked for them, and he did not find them, because they were not there to be found. The all-knowing one went looking for what he already knew, and let the question hang unanswered in the air.

So the day ended with the sandbank empty and the Lord of all worlds standing alone at the water's edge, knowing everything and letting the thing play out a little longer. The mothers of Vrindavan were about to learn that their sons had vanished. And Krishna was about to show the creator something he had not thought to look for.
reflection: Brahma's test is born not of malice but of wonder: the maker of the universe, unable to account for what he has seen, hides the children away simply to understand what is standing before him. The episode quietly reverses the roles, so that the one who tests is himself the one about to be taught.
next_story_tease: But Krishna would not leave the boys' mothers to grieve for long.
hero_scene: An empty sandbank by the river at dusk, with the boys' half-eaten meal spread on the ground and the boy Krishna standing alone at the water's edge — the only figure left in a landscape from which every calf and cowherd boy has vanished.
